analysis.one_liner: Requires workplace chemical hazard safety sheets to be written in both English and Spanish.
analysis.headline: A bill to require bilingual chemical safety sheets in workplaces never got a hearing or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Occupational Safety and Health Act to require chemical manufacturers and importers to produce safety data sheets — the documents that list a chemical's hazards and how to handle it safely — in both English and Spanish, and to make them accessible to the workers exposed to the hazard. It was sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Millions of workers who handle hazardous chemicals but read Spanish better than English would get safety instructions they can actually understand. That includes many workers in agriculture, construction, meatpacking, cleaning, and manufacturing.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the OSH Act so that OSHA standards must require safety data sheets for hazardous chemicals to be produced in English and Spanish by the chemical manufacturer or importer, provided to employers, and made accessible to exposed employees [S2].
It applies to any OSHA standard issued or modified under section 6(b) starting 60 days after enactment, so the requirement would reach existing as well as new standards [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Chemical manufacturers and importers, who would have to produce and maintain every safety data sheet in two languages, and employers, who would have to keep the bilingual sheets accessible to exposed workers.

drawbacks.text: Chemical manufacturers and importers would bear the cost of translating and maintaining safety data sheets in a second language, a cost that is small for large firms but could weigh on small specialty importers [S2].

A translation requirement only helps workers who read Spanish; it does nothing for workers literate in other languages, and translated sheets can contain errors or become outdated unless both versions are kept in sync [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but targeted: Spanish-language safety information directly affects whether a worker can understand what chemicals can hurt them and what to do in an emergency. The cost to industry is translation and document management, which is modest relative to existing hazard-communication duties, but the bill is silent on accuracy of translations and on workers who read neither language.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Henry Cuellar (D-TX) introduced the bill on July 11, 2024 [S1].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce [S4].
No further action was ever recorded: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote [S4].
Three House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Chemical manufacturers and importers are better off because the bilingual labeling requirement never became law; Spanish-speaking workers got no new access to safety information in a language they read.

for.name: Rep. Henry Cuellar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require English- and Spanish-language chemical safety data sheets.

against.name: Rep. Virginia Foxx
against.role: Chair, House Education and Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Her committee received the bill on referral and took no action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no opposition was recorded; the sponsor was a Democrat, all three cosponsors were Democrats, and the committee controlled by Republicans simply never acted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would require them to produce every safety data sheet in English and Spanish and hand it to employers. Their interest in avoiding that compliance cost runs directly against Spanish-speaking workers' ability to read hazard warnings.

industries.industry: Employers with hazardous-chemical workforces (agriculture, construction, cleaning, manufacturing)
industries.note: Employers would have to keep bilingual sheets accessible to exposed workers, a modest administrative burden; workers who can finally understand the warnings are less likely to be hurt on the job.
